title: Akira Ransomware Gang Reboots Systems Into Safe Mode to Kill Security Tools, but Breaks Own Encryptor
excerpt: In a twist of irony, the prolific ransomware group's latest tactic successfully disabled endpoint defenses but caused its own encryption payload to fail, leaving stolen data as its only leverage.
body:
• Akira ransomware operators rebooted victim systems into Windows Safe Mode to disable endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools before attempting encryption.
  • The tactic backfired: while Safe Mode disabled security software, it also broke Akira's own encryptor, preventing file encryption.
  • The attackers still managed to exfiltrate data, falling back on data-theft extortion rather than the traditional encrypt-and-ransom approach.
  • Akira has collected over $42 million in ransom payments and compromised more than 300 organizations worldwide since emerging in March 2023.

Safe Mode as a Weapon — and a Liability

Security researchers have documented a new Akira ransomware campaign in which the gang rebooted compromised systems into Windows Safe Mode — a minimal diagnostic state where most third-party software, including endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, does not load. The technique was designed to clear the way for unimpeded encryption.

https://x.com/Dinosn/status/2087541562389492211

The approach has precedent. The Snatch ransomware group pioneered Safe Mode reboots for EDR evasion in 2019, and Black Basta has used similar tactics. But Akira's implementation came with an unintended consequence: the group's own encryption binary also failed to execute properly in Safe Mode's stripped-down environment.

The result was a partial attack. Akira's operators successfully disabled victim defenses and stole data, but could not lock files. They fell back on data-theft extortion — threatening to publish stolen information unless a ransom was paid — rather than the double-extortion model that has been their signature.

How the Attack Unfolded

Akira affiliates have been gaining initial access primarily through compromised SonicWall SSL VPN credentials, a vector the group has exploited aggressively since mid-2025. In recent campaigns, attackers used stolen or brute-forced VPN credentials to enter corporate networks, then moved laterally using Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) and tools like AnyDesk and Impacket.

The attackers attempted to configure systems to boot into Safe Mode with networking enabled, which would allow network access while still disabling most security software. When EDR tools detected and blocked the ransomware payload in normal mode, the operators escalated to the Safe Mode reboot technique.

In prior campaigns, Akira has used Bring Your Own Vulnerable Driver (BYOVD) attacks, loading a legitimate Intel CPU tuning driver (rwdrv.sys from ThrottleStop) to gain kernel-level access and then deploying a malicious driver (hlpdrv.sys) to modify Windows Defender's registry settings. The Safe Mode approach represents an escalation in the cat-and-mouse game with defenders.

A Growing Threat With a Long Trail

Akira emerged in March 2023 and has rapidly become one of the most prolific ransomware operations globally. According to the FBI and CISA, the group collected over $42 million in ransom payments from more than 250 victims by April 2024, with the total now significantly higher. Microsoft's most recent Digital Defense Report ranked Akira as the top ransomware variant, responsible for 17% of all attacks.

The group's victim list includes Nissan's Oceania and Australia operations, Hitachi Vantara, Stanford University, and numerous organizations across healthcare, government, and critical infrastructure. Ransom demands range from $200,000 to several million dollars depending on the target's size.

"The most crucial mitigation is to reset all SSL VPN credentials on SonicWall devices that have ever run firmware vulnerable to CVE-2024-40766."

— Arctic Wolf Labs, cybersecurity advisory

What Organizations Should Do

The Safe Mode incident underscores that no single defensive layer is sufficient. Security teams should monitor for unexpected Safe Mode boot configurations, implement network segmentation to limit lateral movement, enforce multi-factor authentication on all VPN and remote access systems, and maintain offline backups that cannot be reached through network-connected systems.

The irony of Akira's failed encryption highlights the fragility of even sophisticated attack toolchains. But organizations should not take comfort in the encryptor's failure — the data was still stolen, and the extortion threat remains fully operational.
